AGENDA
  BLUE RIBBON PENSION REVIEW COMMITTEE
  VIA TELECONFERENCE ONLY
 Meetings are broadcast live on Glendale TV, viewable on Spectrum Cable, channel 6, and AT&T U-
 verse, channel 99. Meetings are also streamed live in high definition (HD) on the city's webpage,
 glendaleca.gov/live, on YouTube.com/myglendale, and on Apple TV, Roku, and Amazon Fire devices
 using a free app called Screenweave and choosing “Glendale TV” from the menu. Meetings are also
 archived on the City Website for viewing anytime at glendaleca.gov/agendas. Call (818) 548-4013 for
 program schedules. DVDs of the proceedings are available for purchase in the City Clerk's Office.
 If you have any question about matters on the agenda, or requests for assistance, please contact the
 Management Services Department at (818) 548-4844, during regular business hours.
  PLEASE TURN OFF CELLULAR PHONES WHILE INSIDE THE MEETING LOCATION
 In compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990, auxiliary hearing aids, sign
 language translation, and Braille transcripts are available upon request. Assisted listening devices
 are available same-day upon request. At least 48 hours (or two business days) notice is required for
 requests regarding sign language translation and Braille transcription services. All documents related
 to open session items on this agenda that are received less than 72 hours prior to this meeting, and
 are public records, will be available for review in the Office of the City Clerk, 613 E. Broadway, RM
 110, Glendale, CA 91206.
 Translation services are provided for meetings through the use of bilingual staff for speakers who
 wish to utilize the service as available. Speakers should state their request by contacting the City
 Clerk’s office at (818) 548-2090, at least 24 hours prior to the scheduled meeting. Please specify
 the language for which you require translation. The exclusive use of City provided interpreters is not
 required and persons are welcome to use their own interpreter or speak in their native language.
  NOVEMBER 15, 2021 AT 6:30 PM

To help slow the transmission of COVID-19, and protect the health and safety of the community, City
Council, as well as Board & Commission meetings, will continue to be closed to the public for in-person
attendance.
The public is encouraged to watch and participate from the safety of their homes to practice social
distancing. Meetings are broadcast live on Glendale TV, viewable on Spectrum Cable, channel 6, and
AT&T U-verse, channel 99. Meetings are also streamed live in high definition (HD) on the city's webpage,
glendaleca.gov/live, on YouTube.com/myglendale, and on Apple TV, Roku, and Amazon Fire devices
using a free app called Screenweave and choosing “Glendale TV” from the menu.
For public comments and questions during the meeting, call (818) 937-8100. Public comments on a
specific agenda item will be taken when that agenda item is discussed.

CITY OF GLENDALE
  BLUE RIBBON PENSION REVIEW COMMITTEE
  REGULAR MEETING MINUTES

  November 15, 2021
ROLL CALL

Meeting starts at: 6:34pm

Present: Amirian, Manning, Finch, Masias, Molano, Palos, Holtzman, Bain, Kedikian,
Wolfson, Michals, Zakarian

Absent: Knights, Nelson, Wenz

Staff: Golanian, Doyle, Takhtalian, Garcia, Flynn, Hayrapetian, Hovsepian

1. REGULAR BUSINESS AGENDA
  a. Report of Recorder, re: Posting of Agenda. Mr. Soghomonyan announces that
  the agenda for the November 15, 2021, Blue Ribbon Pension Review Committee
  was Posted on November 12, 2021, on the Bulletin Board Outside City Hall.

2. ORAL COMMUNICATIONS
  None

  Wolfson requests that Committee members have the option to make comments
  on each agenda item and notes that Committee members have not had enough
  time to raise questions in the past. She also notes that she does not think the
  Committee is on track to reach the Committee’s stated goal by the time January
  is over.

3. MINUTES
  a. Approval of the minutes of the Regular Meeting on October 18, 2021.

  Molano amends the minutes from the last session, noting that he expressed a
  concern that was not accurately reported. The concern is that congress may
  increase or do away with the limit on the level at which one gets taxed for social
  security, which is tied to the cap on pensionable compensation for PEPRA
  employees. If congress increases the former, it may increase the City’s pension
  obligation by raising the cap on pensionable compensation for PEPRA
  employees.

  Wolfson requests that Committee Members be allowed to raise questions at the
  top of agenda items rather than before.

  1
   Manning moves to approve the minutes as amended
  Seconded by Amirian

  Motion passes unanimously

4.BUSINESS ITEMS
  a. Public Comments from Committee Members

  Holtzman addresses Ms. Wolfson speaking to City Council in open session in a
  way that could be construed as speaking on behalf of the Committee.

  Garcia asks that members make sure they’re clear that they’re speaking for
  themselves and not the Committee.

  Wolfson acknowledges that she made an error in identifying herself as a member
  of the Committee in the meeting with City Council. She notes that she stands by
  the content of what she said during that meeting. Wolfson notes that in other
  Committees, there are not time limits on meetings.

  Zakarian thanks everyone for spending time on meetings and he thanks Wolfson
  for apologizing. He adds that the Committee is an advisory body, and that the
  Committee has an effect on how the public sees the City’s pension obligations.

  Kedikian notes that materials he sent to Holtzman were not voted on as a future
  agenda item by the Executive Committee in previous Executive Committee
  meeting.

  Molano responds that he did bring up Kedikian’s items during the Executive
  Committee meeting.

  Manning adds that there is an agenda item in regular meetings to add items to
  future agendas. He notes that just because something was not discussed during
  an Executive Committee meeting does not mean it cannot be agendized.

  Takhtalian discusses Wolfson’s questions regarding the GMA MOU and the
  City’s contribution rate. Takhtalian clarifies that the City does not pay any of the
  employee contribution to PERS.

  Wolfson notes that the MOU says employee contribution, not employer
  contribution.

  Takhtalian notes that the employee contribution is 8% plus cost share, where the
  employee picks up a portion of the employer’s contribution.

  2
   Flynn adds that its very similar if not the same as social security.

  Public Comment: Mike Mohill states that he does not think Amirian should be on
  the Committee.

b. Conclusion of Redding’s PPT Presentation

  Redding discusses PEPRA pay limits. The limit was originally established by
  tying it to the social security limit, but after that time it is no longer tired to the
  social security limit, so any changes to social security will not affect the PEPRA
  limits.

  Redding continues her presentation about what can be done by the City
  regarding unfunded liability, including:
  1) Pay more money to CalPERS sooner
  2) 115 Trusts
  3) Pension Obligation Bonds (POBs)
  4) Requesting shorter amortization period
  5) Additional discretionary payments (ADP)

  Holtzman asks: is termination likely to be a good financial bet? He notes that
  current UAL is $645 million, and if that’s paid off with a POB, unlike with
  termination, City could have to pay again. He adds that with termination, the City
  would have to pay off the $2.8 Billion, but the City would be done.

  Redding notes that the City’s General Fund revenue is approx. 250 million, which
  suggests that the City could payoff pension liability in 2-3 years if it didn’t expend
  revenue on anything else. She adds that if City were to terminate, the City would
  not really be done in the pension business because CA rules holds that all
  employees have a vested right to retirement benefit. So, the City would have to
  start up a new pension plan for all existing employees. Redding thinks it would be
  better to pay the $645 and take the risk.

  Holtzman asks Redding to explain POBs and what the risks are.

  Redding explains that in the past year, interest rates were really low. She notes
  that she cannot predict how long that will last, but in the current environment
  Cities have opportunity to borrow at 3%. So, the current environment has made
  POBs more popular. She adds that this can go bad because even if City gets
  3%, the City has to hope that CalPERS doesn’t earn less than 3% in the long
  term. The other issue is that if CalPERS loses 25% of money, the City will owe
  that to CalPERS and still have to pay the POB. If the City’s plan becomes 100%

  3
 funded, the City still has to pay normal cost. In the same environment, with a
POB the City has to pay bond holders even is investments did really well.
Redding estimates that a POB is a good deal somewhere between 75% and 85%
of the time.

Holtzman notes that he is seeing more jurisdictions using POBs.

Holtzman asks about the connection between compensation levels and pension
liabilities. He notes that in a commonsense way, final compensation sets the
pension benefit, and so one would think that the higher the final compensation,
the higher the pension benefit. Is reducing compensation a way to reduce
pension obligation?

Redding responds that this is a hard question. A lot of unfunded liability is related
to retirees. So, reducing compensation only affects part of the unfunded liability.
Whatever actuaries project, the actuary calculations are based on what actually
happens, and the actuaries true up every year. Decreasing pay will decrease
cost next year, but the issue is whether Cities can keep wage lower like that in
the long-term. Cities might get away with lower salaries for a short period of time,
but in the long run it doesn’t work because Cities will lose employees.

Wolfson states that, in theory, returns should be better from CalPERS because
they don’t have profit motive, but their performance just isn’t stellar. Because of
this, she is not sure why the Committee should assume that the City would get a
better rate of return from CalPERS than elsewhere.

Wolfson asks how CalPERS holds agencies to the 7% rate?

Redding notes that the June 30, 2020, numbers have changed quite a bit. She
adds that the reason CalPERS charges 7% interest is because they have to
charge the rate set by the Board as the discount rate.

Wolfson asks Redding to clarify the differences between POBs and irrevocable
trusts.

Redding responds that POBs are a way of borrowing a relatively large amount of
money with the condition that borrower will use that money to pay off pension
debt. Once you give that money to CalPERS, you are betting that CalPERS will
do well with that money. In contrast, the City could set up a 115 trust to hold
money until the City thinks it’s a good time to give that money to CalPERS. A
POB is a way to get money that must go to CalPERS.

  4
 Molano asks about 115 trusts: can the City set aside money for purposes of
having funds in the event that it pursues layoffs as a way of reducing its pension
obligations?

Redding responds no, it has to be used for paying off the CalPERS pension
obligation.

Molano asks whether Redding’s background allows her to speak to the feasibility
of reducing or putting a cap on pay for employees.

Redding responds that her experience is that when agencies try to reduce
compensation, they have major labor issues with hiring and retention.

Masias asks why there were preset allocations in the 115 trusts. He adds that
having a profit motive would be better than having CalPERS in charge. In the
years that CalPERS has done well are years when everyone has done well.

Redding notes that the 115 trust providers are PARS, PFM and Keenan
CEPPT. She adds that with preset trusts, the strategies are designed to be
conservative.

Masias says that it seems like CalPERS is trying to be punitive with agencies that
are trying to move away from their system. He notes that in private sector,
employees can only put away $19,000 into 401k, and that in contrast public
employees are making out like bandits on retirement benefits.

Flynn notes that the City’s 115 plan is controlled by PARS; Highmark is the
investment manager; the trust balance is shy of $41 million; annualized net return
is about 6%. The plan is in a moderate portfolio: about 52% equities and fixed
income and cash is the remainder. So, it’s similar to the PERS strategies offered.
PARS offers more strategies than the two strategies, but the City Council wanted
a moderate trust.

Kedikian notes that he may be an outlier regarding his opinion on the $2.8 billion
termination cost. He states that CalPERS doesn’t have any obligation to the
taxpayer and asks why then, does the City have to follow the numbers they
provide? He asks if CalPERS has any legal basis to ask for everything up front,
and whether it has any legal basis for the numbers it provides. He adds that he
would like the Committee to check and verify the demands to see if they’re legal
and if they can or cannot be challenged. He requests a complete CalPERS
agreement with the City and for an expert come in and tell us what can and
cannot be challenged therein.

  5
 Holtzman notes that he will try to find someone to address this. He provides a
short answer: the contract says we will abide by CalPERS’ rules, and they have
various options for remedies.
Redding notes that a large number of public agencies have been trying to figure
out ways to get out of CalPERS, which isn’t to say that it cannot be done.

Holtzman adds that the problem beyond the City’s contractual obligation to
CalPERS, is that CalPERS would take it out on the City’s employees and would
have the option to go after the City’s assets.

Wolfson asks: why can’t multiple cities band together to negotiate better terms
with CalPERS?

Holtzman notes that there are legislative actions that could help. For example,
the constitution doesn’t hold that CalPERS has any fiduciary duty to cities, but
they do have duty to employees (members). He notes that in partial defense of
CalPERS, the best argument of is that CalPERS has not lowered the discount
rate more quickly because they don’t want to bankrupt the people who have been
paying. But CalPERS has a board and when cities show up en masse they can
have an impact.

Redding adds that the League of California Cities is a vocal entity in CalPERS
negotiations.

Wolfson notes that she thinks CalPERS is often dictatorial and rules by fiat.

Holtzman notes Wolfson is not alone in that view.

Redding adds that another response to the City’s pension obligation is to not take
any action. If the City is comfortable with where the costs are going, the City
does not have to do anything. That’s an OK choice too.

Holtzman thanks Redding for her presentation

Bain notes that one of the items not mentioned was difference in assumptions
between ongoing plan and termination; CalPERS is shifting from being a
custodian of funds to an insurer of benefits. So, when Cities withdraw, CalPERS
is on the hook to others and promising to cover the benefits. The low
assumptions are very similar to what insurance companies use to cover annuity
payments.

Kedikian notes that the group should discuss whether CalPERS can shift the rate
without giving the City an option to discuss. If CalPERS is going in the direction

  6
   of being an insurer maybe the City has the opportunity to get out of their
  agreement with CalPERS.

  Molano notes that today we addressed what options the City has going forward,
  assuming the structure of PEPRA going forward will not change. He adds that if
  the Committee doesn’t address how the City gets into MOUs, then the
  Committee will only address portion of the problem.

5. REPORTS
  None.

6. REQUESTS FOR ITEMS ON FUTURE AGENDAS
  None.

7. ADJOURNMENT
  Kedikian moves to adjourn.
  Manning seconds.

  Meeting adjourns at 8:32pm

  7
